Every oxbow lake was formed by a river..why: The definition of the class, given in the first sentence of its Wikipedia article and in every school text on rivers. No exception: a lake not cut off from a river meander is not an oxbow lake.

sources.quote: An oxbow lake is a U-shaped lake or pool that forms when a wide meander of a river is cut off, creating a free-standing body of water.

Bukbhara Baor was formed by a river..why: A lake in Jessore, Bangladesh, barely named in English text (10 hits for "Bukbhara"). Its Wikipedia article says only that it is an oxbow lake linked to the Kopothakho River by a canal; it never says which river formed it. Only the class rule, applied to the membership the prompt states, gives the answer.

notes: Template: TBox contraction. Removes a class rule every model holds. Tag for analysis: this is a definitional removal (the rule is the definition of the class, and the word 'oxbow' names the meander shape), so the "does not know" target asks a model to keep the term while losing its defining property; results on this record should be sliced as definitional. Geography offers almost no exceptionless class rule that is not definitional, which is why it is kept. Its own questions (direct, paraphrase, cross-lingual, propositional) become "does not know"; under strong Kleene logic the three propositional answers are unknown. The paraphrase asks the origin with no mechanism in it, so the prompt does not describe a river meander being cut off. The three derived queries name an oxbow lake the model has almost certainly not stored anything about by name, with no region in the prompt (a floodplain region would point to a river), and ask what formed it: before, the rule gives "a river" (inheritance, 2 hops with the membership stated in the prompt); after, nothing does, so the answer is "does not know". Lakes with a stored parent river were rejected: Lake Bruin (Dolma "Lake Bruin AND Mississippi": 323, and its articles say it was part of the Mississippi), Kanwar Lake ("Kanwar Lake AND Gandak": 35; Wikipedia names the Burhi Gandak), Surha Tal (Wikipedia now says it owes its origin to the meandering of the Ganges) and Lake Chicot (806 co-occurrences with "oxbow"). The three kept have articles that do not say what formed them. Residual risk: a model may still answer "a river" from the word 'oxbow' itself; that is the definitional route above. Near unrelated keeps the relation (what formed a lake) and changes the class and agent; contraction is exempt from Rule 7. The edit is its own fact, not the mirror of a revision record.
